messages.subject: Re: Nimble model formulation of DPM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Meng,

I don't know whether you have already received some private replies about this.

It seems to me you may have some misunderstanding in how Dirichlet-process mixture models are implemented? For Monte Carlo sampling one typically introduces "cluster-occupation" variables (the literature uses many different names for these). There's one cluster-occupation variable per datapoint: the value of each variable says to which cluster its respective datapoint belongs to. In your enclosed example, "xi" is such a variable. For example, if xi[2]==5, then it means that datapoint #2 belongs to cluster #5, and therefore it uses the lambda-vector belonging to cluster five: lambda[5,j]. In the code you see this because at iteration i=2 we'd have

       y[2, j] ~ dpois( lambda[xi[2],  j] )

and since in our example xi[2]==5, this effectively means

       y[2, j] ~ dpois( lambda[5,  j] )

Check out the Nimble manual (https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-welcome-nimble.html) around § 10.2, especially the explanation in § 10.2.1.2.

For Dirichlet-process mixtures of Gaussians there are several good introductory articles explaining this; for example a review by West & al. that should still be freely available here:

http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.49.2449

check out § 2 there.

My sincere apologies if I misunderstood your problem and what I said was already clear or trivial to you!

Cheers,
Luca

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luca,

Hope you had a good Halloween weekend. And thanks a lot for your reply.

The reason why I asked the question is that nimble did not create the clustering of the parameters in the following DP mixture of product of Bernoullis model:

library(poLCA)
data(values)
values[values==2] <- 0  # replace 2 with 0
data <- list(y = values)

library(nimble)
code <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:n] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = n)
  alpha ~ dgamma(shape = 1, rate = 1)

  for(i in 1:n) {
    for(j in 1:J) {

      y[i, j] ~ dbern(p[z[i], j])

    }
  }

  for(i in 1:n) {
    for(j in 1:J) {

      p[i, j] ~ dbeta(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5)
    }
  }
})

n <- nrow(data$y)
J <- ncol(data$y)
constants <- list(n = n, J = J)
set.seed(123)
inits <- list(alpha = 1, p = matrix(rbeta(n*J, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5), nrow = n, ncol = J),
              z = sample(1:5, size = constants$n, replace = TRUE))
model <- nimbleModel(code, data=data, inits = inits, constants = constants,
                     dimensions = list(p = c(n, J)))
cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
conf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = c('z', 'p', 'alpha'), print = TRUE)
mcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
cmcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc, project = model)
samples <- runMCMC(cmcmc,  niter=25000, nburnin = 5000, thin=10)

zSamples <- samples[, grep('z', colnames(samples))]    # samples of cluster IDs
nGroups <- apply(zSamples, 1, function(x)  length(unique(x)))
concSamples <- samples[, grep('alpha', colnames(samples))]
pSamples <- samples[, grep('p', colnames(samples))]
pSamples <- pSamples[, -1]   # remove "alpha"
table(pSamples[1, 1:n])   # check the clustering of p of variable 1 for iteration 1

My understanding is that, for each iteration, clustering should be induced by CRP for samples of parameters. However, after using the table function in the last line of my code, I found that all the values were different. Is there anything wrong with my code?

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: ICAR model with NaN WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nimble experts,

Hope you had a great weekend.

I am trying to fit a very simple model, and I have updated the nimble package, but still got NaN WAIC value. I appreciate it if anyone could help me with this issue. Many thanks. Please see the code below. Best, Vicky.

ICARCode<-nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:N){

    icedata[i]~T(dnorm(u[i], tau),-1,1)#in R only this form can be used

    u[i]<-alpha+phi[i]

  }

  phi[1:N]~dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau.phi, zero_mean = 1)

  #alpha~dflat()
  alpha~dnorm(0,tau0)
  tau0~dgamma(2,0.5)
  tau.phi~dgamma(2,0.5)
  tau~dgamma(2,0.5)
  #tau.theta~dgamma(0.5,0.0005)

})

inits1<- list(alpha=0.01,
              tau=0.01,
              tau.phi=0.1,
              phi=rep(0.01,67),
              tau0=0.01)

params1<-c('alpha','phi','tau','tau.phi')

ICARCodesamples <- nimbleMCMC(code = ICARCode,
                             data = I,
                             constants = constant,
                             inits = inits1,
                             monitors = params1,
                             niter = 10000,
                             nburnin = 6000,
                             thin = 10,
                             nchains = 1,
                             setSeed = 1234,
                             progressBar = FALSE,
                             samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
                             summary = TRUE,
                             WAIC = TRUE
)

The warning message: There are individual pWAIC values that are greater than 0.4. This may indicate that the WAIC estimate is unstable (Vehtari et al., 2017), at least in cases without grouping of data nodes or multivariate data nodes.

messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble users/developers,

I received some help getting the sampler_RJ_indicator function to work for a problem where I wanted to select among both categorical and continuous variables and have the algorithm sample the categorical variable as one variable (although it is represented by multiple indicator variables in the model).

This seemed to work fine in the last version of nimble that I have on my PC, but when I updated the version and tried to run it on my Mac it fails to compile and reports the error that is related to a modified version of the sampler_RJ_indicator that I created with some help (thanks Sally!).

I get this error related to the custom sampler (my_sampler_RJ_indicator):

mcmc5 = compileNimble(mcmc, project = RJexampleModel, resetFunctions = TRUE, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)
Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] On some systems there may be some compiler warnings that can be safely ignored.
Error : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
Error: There is some problem at the Eigen processing step for this code:

I'm not sure why the code would run fine in a previous version and now it is throwing this error. The inner workings of nimble are a bit over my head, so I was hoping this would be more obvious to someone involved with the development.

Here is the example code that I was trying to run the function with:

## example MCMC rj

# my_sampler_RJ_indicator #######################################
my_sampler_RJ_indicator <- nimbleFunction(
  name = 'my_sampler_RJ_indicator',
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    ## note: target is the indicator variable,
    ## control$targetNode is the variable conditionally in the model
    ## control list extraction
    coefNode      <- model$expandNodeNames(control$targetNode, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
    coefNodes     <- control$targetNode
    proposalScale <- control$scale
    proposalMean  <- control$mean
    ## node list generation
    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(c(coefNode, target))
    calcNodesReduced <- model$getDependencies(target)
  },
  run = function() {
    currentIndicator <- model[[target]]
    if(currentIndicator == 0) {   ## propose addition of coefNode
      currentLogProb <- model$getLogProb(calcNodesReduced)
      proposalCoef <- numeric(length(coefNode))
      logProbForwardProposal <- 0
      for(l in 1:length(coefNode)){
        proposalCoef[l] <- rnorm(1, proposalMean, proposalScale)
        logProbForwardProposal <- logProbForwardProposal + dnorm(proposalCoef[l], proposalMean, proposalScale, log = TRUE)
      }
      model[[coefNodes]] <<- proposalCoef
      model[[target]] <<- 1
      proposalLogProb <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
      logAcceptanceProb <- proposalLogProb - currentLogProb - logProbForwardProposal
    } else {                      ## propose removal of coefNode
      currentLogProb <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)
      currentCoef <-  model[[coefNodes]]
      logProbReverseProposal<- 0
      for(l in 1:length(coefNode)){
        logProbReverseProposal <- logProbReverseProposal + dnorm(currentCoef[l], proposalMean, proposalScale, log = TRUE)
      }
      model[[coefNodes]] <<- 0
      model[[target]] <<- 0
      model$calculate(calcNodes)
      logAcceptanceProb <- model$getLogProb(calcNodesReduced) - currentLogProb + logProbReverseProposal
    }
    accept <- decide(logAcceptanceProb)
    if(accept) { copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
    } else     { copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE) }
  },
  methods = list(
    reset = function() { }
  )
)

code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta[1] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta[2] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta[3] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
  for(i in 1:2){
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
  }
  #z1 ~ dbern(psi)  ## indicator variable associated with beta1
  #z2 ~ dbern(psi)  ## indicator variable associated with beta2
  psi ~ dbeta(1, 1) ## hyperprior on inclusion probability
  for(i in 1:N) {
    Ypred[i] <- beta0 + z[1]*beta[1] * x1[i] + z[1] *beta[2] * x2[i] + beta[3] * x3[i] * z[2]
    Y[i] ~ dnorm(Ypred[i], sd = sigma)
  }
})

## simulate some data
set.seed(1)
N <- 100
x1 <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)
x2 <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.5) #
x3 = std2(runif(N, -10, 10))
Y <- rnorm(N, 1.5 + 2 * x1 + 0.4 * x2 + 0.8 * x3, sd = 1)

## build the model and configure default MCMC

RJexampleModel <- nimbleModel(code, constants = list(N = N),
                              data = list(Y = Y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3=x3),
                              inits = list(beta0 = 0, beta=c(0,0,0),
                                           sigma = sd(Y), z = rbinom(2,1,0.5), psi = 0.5))
cRJexampleModel <- compileNimble(RJexampleModel)

RJexampleConf <- configureMCMC(RJexampleModel)

configureRJ(conf = RJexampleConf,
            targetNodes = c("beta[3]"),
            indicatorNodes = c('z[2]'),
            control = list(mean = c(0), scale = 2))

nodeControl  = list(mean = 0, scale = 1)
nodeControl$targetNode <- c("beta[1:2]")

RJexampleConf$removeSamplers("z[1]")
RJexampleConf$addSampler(type = my_sampler_RJ_indicator,
                target = "z[1]",
                control = nodeControl)

currentConf <- RJexampleConf$getSamplers("beta[1]")
RJexampleConf$removeSampler("beta[1]")
RJexampleConf$addSampler(type = sampler_RJ_toggled,
                         target = "beta[1]",
                         control = list(samplerType = currentConf[[1]]))

currentConf <- RJexampleConf$getSamplers("beta[2]")
RJexampleConf$removeSampler("beta[2]")
RJexampleConf$addSampler(type = sampler_RJ_toggled,
                         target = "beta[2]",
                         control = list(samplerType = currentConf[[1]]))

mpleConf$printSamplers()

RJexampleConf$addMonitors(c('z'))

mcmc = buildMCMC(RJexampleConf)

cmcmc5 = compileNimble(mcmc, project = RJexampleModel, resetFunctions = TRUE, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

#tic()
results_samplerRJind <- runMCMC(cmcmc4, niter = 20000, nburnin=5000,thin=1,nchains=1, setSeed = 500)

Thanks!

Sincerely,

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: ICAR model with NaN WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicky,

This would probably be caused by having a likelihood value that is NaN for at least one posterior sample of the parameters and one or more of the observations.

One possibility is that the zero_mean=1 argument is affecting things. This causes the mean of 'u' to be set to 0 after sampling new values of the individual u[i]. However, it's possible that doing that causes the truncation constraint to no longer be satisfied (though I think you should get -Inf, not NaN in that case). So you might try removing alpha from the model and leaving zero_mean at its default value of 0. On a related note, I'll say that you can't really estimate tau0 from the data, as it is informed only by the value of alpha0, which is a scalar and therefore not really informative about a variance parameter. So, just having the mean of the ICAR be estimated implicitly by the mean of the 'u' values is probably a better strategy.

If that's not the issue, one thing you could do is set up the individual steps of creating the model using nimbleModel() and running the MCMC via runMCMC(), making sure to monitor the 'u' and 'tau' variables. You could then take individual posterior samples of those variables and assign them into the model like this:

nodes <- model$getDependencies(c('u','tau'))  # this will include the icedata nodes and any other child nodes of 'u' and 'tau', which should just be the hidden node representing the standard deviation
model$tau <- out[iteration, 'tau']
model$u <- out[iteration, <columns with u values>]
model$calculate(nodes)

to see if you can find the iterations for which the log-likelihood is NaN.

If you're able to share the data so that we can reproduce the error (either on the list or off-list), I can also take a closer look.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I think the model code is correct, but that the last line of your code does not do what you intended to do. As Luca mentioned, there is one variable in the model that encodes the clustering, that in your case is the `z`. In your code, nGroups give the number of clusters at each iteration, and that is way less than n.

To check the values of p[1:n, 1] at iteration 1 you need to consider the values of the z that tells which clusters observations belong to; then to get what you were looking for you may want to run:

table(pSamples[1, zSamples[1,]])

While, for example, if you want to monitor the how the values for p[1,1] changes across iterations:

plot(pSamples[zSamples[,1],1], type = "l")

Hope this helps!

Best,

Sally

messages.body_snippet:

messages.subject: Re: SCR clustering - issues with indexing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jo,

I had to do a small amount of work to your code to get it to read in as you need to index the list in edf.martin:

edf.marten.C1 <- edf.marten[[1]] %>% filter(Grid_Num < 21)
edf.marten.C2 <- edf.marten[[2]] %>% filter(Grid_Num > 20)

The main problem in your code (which it seems there are a number of issues) for the dbinom_vector distribution was that the dimensions of trials was wrong in the function.

The idea with the vectorization of the binomial is that you have K occasions which are the trials. You can speed up the MCMC by using this vecorization, but you have to tell it how many trials went on for each occasion at each trap. In your example K=4.

So, you need to include the indexing in your data y:

y[i,1:J,g]

and not loop over J in the data, and then trials is just a vector:

y[i,1:J,g] ~ dbinom_vector(size = trials[1:J], prob = p[i,1:J,g])

You're also treating the latent inclusion state (z) as known data in this model and that's incorrect as well because it is a latent parameter.

Also, your calculation for the distance was incorrect. You needed to take the square root after squaring each of the distances between traps and latent AC's.

Finally, I'm not sure what detection function you were going for, but it seemed maybe incorrect. I included the half-normal in there for now, but it's possible that you were using a different function.

Also, I've included a function to give you better starting locations for the latent AC's.

I'm guessing you're coming over from JAGS as I can see that you don't provide initial values for the model or separate constants from data. Also, it's best not to name the latent activity center coordinates as (X) since this is generally reserved for traps in this models; not a big deal.

Finally, there are a couple of other tricks you can use to speed up these models: block sampling latent activity center coordinates and separating the data augmentation step into 2 steps where only the data for detected individuals are included in the observation likelihood.

Anyhow, your code runs fine now:

#####################################################################################
##################------ CURRENT DATA ------##################
#####################################################################################
# run for 2 clusters of marten grid cells
load("MartenGridData_2020.Rda")

# just marten cells
J <- martenGrid.hsdata$J  # 2 clusters of 20 traps each
area <- c(martenGrid.hsdata$area[[1]],martenGrid.hsdata$area[[2]])
xlim <- array(0,c(2,2))
xlim[1,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim[[1]]
xlim[2,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim[[2]]
# xlim <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim

ylim <- array(0,c(2,2))
ylim[1,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim[[1]]
ylim[2,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim[[2]]
# ylim <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim

traps <- array(0,c(J,2,2))
traps.C1 <- as.matrix(martenGrid.hsdata$traps[[1]][,c("x","y")])
traps[,,1] <- traps.C1
traps.C2 <- as.matrix(martenGrid.hsdata$traps[[2]][,c("x","y")])
traps[,,2] <- traps.C2

edf.marten <- martenGrid.hsdata$edf
trials <- cbind(rep(4,20),rep(4,20))
sex <- martenGrid.hsdata$sex
G <- 2 # 2 clusters
M <- 200 # augmented population

# traps are in 2 clusters: 1-20, 21-40
plot(traps[[1]])
plot(traps[[2]])

# y for Cluster 1
y.C1 <- array(0, dim = c(M, 20, 4)) # augmented pop = 200, 20 traps and 4 occasions
# Add the captures as 1s with the good old cbind trick.
edf.marten.C1 <- edf.marten[[1]] %>% filter(Grid_Num < 21)
y.C1[cbind(edf.marten.C1$Animal_Num,edf.marten.C1$Grid_Num, edf.marten.C1$Occ)] <- 1
sum(y.C1) == nrow(edf.marten.C1)     # 6 detections = 3 animals, 1 with 3 detections, 1 with 2 and 1 with 1

# get rid of zeros so observed animals come first
y.C1 = y.C1[which(apply(y.C1,1,sum)>0),,]

# y for Cluster 2
y.C2 <- array(0, dim = c(M, 20, 4)) # augmented pop = 200, 20 traps and 4 occasions
# Add the captures as 1s with the good old cbind trick.
edf.marten.C2 <- edf.marten[[2]] %>% filter(Grid_Num > 20)

y_all[1:n0[2],,2] <- y_all.C2

  psi ~ dbeta(1,1)
  p0 ~ dunif(0,1)

  for(g in 1:G){
    for(i in 1:M){
      z[i,g] ~ dbern(psi)
      s[i,1,g]~dunif(0,20) # traps are centered and scaled, start at 0 and end <20 for both xlim and ylim
      s[i,2,g]~dunif(0,20)

dim(y_all)

scrR$calculate()
scrR$initializeInfo()

Daniel

messages.subject: nimSummary function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm not sure if this function would be useful to you, but I thought I'd share it. It summarizes the MCMC output for model runs with >1 chain. You can choose to exclude certain parameters from the output, for instance, if you don't want one summarize that has many dimensions. So, if your parameter "z" has three dimensions (e.g., z[1, 1, 1], z[1, 1, 1], etc..), you can just request:

nimSummary(mcmcOutput, exclude.params = "z")

Hopefully it runs for you:

nimSummary = function(d = NULL, trace=FALSE, exclude.params = NULL, digits=3){
  if(is.null(exclude.params)==FALSE){
    require(stringr)
    tmp1 = ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(as.numeric(str_extract(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]],"[1-9]+"))),attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]],substr(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]],1,as.numeric(str_locate(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]], "\\[")[, 1])-1))
    d.remove = lapply(d, function(x) which(tmp1 %in% exclude.params))
    d2 = lapply(d, function(x) x[,-d.remove[[1]]])
  }else
    if(is.null(exclude.params)){
      d2 = d
      d.remove = list()
      d.remove = 0
    }
  if((length(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]])-length(d.remove[[1]])==1)){
    d3 = as.data.frame(do.call(c, d2))
    #d3 = d3[,-which(apply(d3, 2, function(x) any(x=="Inf")))]
    Means = mean(d3[,1], na.rm=TRUE)
    SDs = sd(d3[,1], na.rm=TRUE)
    q2.5 = quantile(d3[,1], 0.025, na.rm=TRUE)
    q50 = quantile(d3[,1], 0.50, na.rm=TRUE)
    q97.5 = quantile(d3[,1], 0.975, na.rm=TRUE)
    over.zero = round(mean(d3[,1]>0),2)
    n.eff = effectiveSize(mcmc.list(lapply(d2, as.mcmc)))
    Rhat = round(gelman.diag(mcmc.list(lapply(d2, as.mcmc)), multivariate = FALSE)[[1]][,1],3)
  }else
    if((length(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]])-length(d.remove[[1]])>1)){
      d3=do.call(rbind,d2)
      #d3 = d3[,-which(apply(d3, 2, function(x) any(x=="Inf")))]
      Means = apply(d3, 2,function(x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE))
      SDs = apply(d3, 2,function(x) sd(x,na.rm=TRUE))
      q2.5 = apply(d3, 2,function(x) quantile(x, 0.025,na.rm=TRUE))
      q50 = apply(d3, 2,function(x) quantile(x, 0.50,na.rm=TRUE))
      q97.5 = apply(d3, 2,function(x) quantile(x, 0.975,na.rm=TRUE))
      over.zero = round(apply(d3, 2, function(x) mean(x>0,na.rm=TRUE)),2)
      n.eff = effectiveSize(mcmc.list(lapply(d2, as.mcmc)))
      Rhat = round(gelman.diag(mcmc.list(lapply(d2, as.mcmc)), multivariate = FALSE)[[1]][,1],3)
    }
  if(trace==TRUE  & (length(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]])-length(d.remove[[1]])>1)){
    par(mfrow=c(ncol(d3),2))
    for(i in 1:ncol(d3)){
      plot(1:dim(d2[[1]])[1],d2[[1]][,i],xlab="iteration",ylab=colnames(d3)[i],type="l",ylim=range(do.call(rbind, lapply(d2,function(x) apply(x, 2, range)))[,i]))
      for(j in 2:length(d2)){
        lines(1:dim(d2[[1]])[1],d2[[j]][,i],xlab="iteration",ylab=colnames(d3)[i],type="l",col="red")
      }
      hist(d3[,i],main="",xlab=colnames(d3)[i])
    }
  }else
    if(trace==TRUE  & (length(attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]])-length(d.remove[[1]])==1)){
      par(mfrow=c(1,2))
      plot(1:length(d2[[1]]),d2[[1]],xlab="iteration",ylab=colnames(d3)[i],type="l",ylim=range(d3[,1]))
      for(j in 2:length(d2)){
        lines(1:length(d2[[j]]),d2[[j]],xlab="iteration",ylab=colnames(d3)[i],type="l",col="red")
      }
      hist(d3[,1],main="",xlab=attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]][-d.remove[[1]]])
    }
  tmp.frame = data.frame(post.mean=Means,post.sd <http://post.sd>=SDs,q2.5=q2.5,q50=q50,q97.5=q97.5,f0=over.zero,n.eff=n.eff,Rhat=Rhat)
  if(nrow(tmp.frame)==1){
    row.names(tmp.frame) = attributes(d[[1]])$dimnames[[2]][-d.remove[[1]]]
  }
  return(round(tmp.frame, digits=digits))
}

Here is some example code I borrowed to test out the function:

library(nimble, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(stringr)

code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)        # prior for variance components based on Gelman (2006)
  for(i in 1:n) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sd = sigma) # manual entry of linear predictors
  }
})

## extract data for two predictors and center for better MCMC performance
x1 <- X[,1] - mean(X[,1])
x2 <- X[,2] - mean(X[,2])

constants <- list(n = n, x1 = x1, x2 = x2)
data <- list(y = y)
inits <- list(beta0 = mean(y), beta1 = 0, beta2 = 0, sigma = 1)
model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits) # build model

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(model)

# compile model to C++#
modelC <- compileNimble(model, showCompilerOutput = F)
# MCMC sampler configurations
# build the MCMC specifications
buildMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
# complile the code in S+
lmMCMCc <- compileNimble(buildMCMC, project = model, resetFunctions = TRUE)
# run MCMC

results1 <- runMCMC(lmMCMCc, niter = 500, nburnin=100,thin=1,nchains=2, setSeed = 500)

# summarize results
nimSummary(results1)
nimSummary(results1, exclude.params = c("sigma"))

Cheers,

Daniel

On Wednesday, November 3, 2021 at 12:02:22 PM UTC-7 taurusw...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Jo,
>
> I had to do a small amount of work to your code to get it to read in as you need to index the list in edf.martin:
>
> edf.marten.C1 <- edf.marten[[1]] %>% filter(Grid_Num < 21)
> edf.marten.C2 <- edf.marten[[2]] %>% filter(Grid_Num > 20)
>
> The main problem in your code (which it seems there are a number of issues) for the dbinom_vector distribution was that the dimensions of trials was wrong in the function.
>
> The idea with the vectorization of the binomial is that you have K occasions which are the trials. You can speed up the MCMC by using this vecorization, but you have to tell it how many trials went on for each occasion at each trap. In your example K=4.
>
> So, you need to include the indexing in your data y:
>
> y[i,1:J,g]
>
> and not loop over J in the data, and then trials is just a vector:
>
> y[i,1:J,g] ~ dbinom_vector(size = trials[1:J], prob = p[i,1:J,g])
>
> You're also treating the latent inclusion state (z) as known data in this model and that's incorrect as well because it is a latent parameter.
>
> Also, your calculation for the distance was incorrect. You needed to take the square root after squaring each of the distances between traps and latent AC's.
>
> Finally, I'm not sure what detection function you were going for, but it seemed maybe incorrect. I included the half-normal in there for now, but it's possible that you were using a different function.
>
> Also, I've included a function to give you better starting locations for the latent AC's.
>
> I'm guessing you're coming over from JAGS as I can see that you don't provide initial values for the model or separate constants from data. Also, it's best not to name the latent activity center coordinates as (X) since this is generally reserved for traps in this models; not a big deal.
>
> Finally, there are a couple of other tricks you can use to speed up these models: block sampling latent activity center coordinates and separating the data augmentation step into 2 steps where only the data for detected individuals are included in the observation likelihood.
>
>
> Anyhow, your code runs fine now:
>
>
> #####################################################################################
> ##################------ CURRENT DATA ------##################
> #####################################################################################
> # run for 2 clusters of marten grid cells
> load("MartenGridData_2020.Rda")
>
> # just marten cells
> J <- martenGrid.hsdata$J  # 2 clusters of 20 traps each
> area <- c(martenGrid.hsdata$area[[1]],martenGrid.hsdata$area[[2]])
> xlim <- array(0,c(2,2))
> xlim[1,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim[[1]]
> xlim[2,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim[[2]]
> # xlim <- martenGrid.hsdata$xlim
>
> ylim <- array(0,c(2,2))
> ylim[1,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim[[1]]
> ylim[2,] <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim[[2]]
> # ylim <- martenGrid.hsdata$ylim
>
> traps <- array(0,c(J,2,2))
> traps.C1 <- as.matrix(martenGrid.hsdata$traps[[1]][,c("x","y")])
> traps[,,1] <- traps.C1
> traps.C2 <- as.matrix(martenGrid.hsdata$traps[[2]][,c("x","y")])
> traps[,,2] <- traps.C2
>
>
> edf.marten <- martenGrid.hsdata$edf
> trials <- cbind(rep(4,20),rep(4,20))
> sex <- martenGrid.hsdata$sex
> G <- 2 # 2 clusters
> M <- 200 # augmented population
>
> # traps are in 2 clusters: 1-20, 21-40
> plot(traps[[1]])
> plot(traps[[2]])
>
> # y for Cluster 1
> y.C1 <- array(0, dim = c(M, 20, 4)) # augmented pop = 200, 20 traps and 4 occasions
> # Add the captures as 1s with the good old cbind trick.
> edf.marten.C1 <- edf.marten[[1]] %>% filter(Grid_Num < 21)
> y.C1[cbind(edf.marten.C1$Animal_Num,edf.marten.C1$Grid_Num, edf.marten.C1$Occ)] <- 1

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

This looks really interesting.  Thanks for posting the question and giving clear code.

Your data setup code gave me an error at:
TraitData <- ConvData(TraitData.tmp, whNum = ToNum)

After some inspection, I did this, I think without harm, to keep moving:
TraitData.tmp <- TraitData.tmp[,-1]

The problem causing those error messages (and crashes) is something we should be error-trapping.  It's an easy mistake for a user to make, and the error information was inscrutable.  It looks like your inits value for alSpeciesSTAR should be length 68 but was length 74. If I am not lost, I think this was from using nrow(dat$Abund) instead of ncol(dat$Abund) in the last step of OrdInits2D.  Having the wrong length inits for alSpeciesSTAR caused a cascade of issues into the block sampler for alSpeciesSTAR (or the one with it as a component).

Another minor issue is that when you compile the model first and the MCMC second, you should include "project = model".  In your code:
HeirOrd2D.CompMCMC <- compileNimble(HeirOrd2D.MCMC, project = HeirOrd2D)

By the way, block samplers in many dimensions may not work well.  There is a control list parameter "tries", which I also noticed recently was left out of help(samplers), that will repeat the propose-accept-reject steps "tries" times, giving more effort into making a move among the many dimensions.  Otherwise the one sampler can often fail to make a move (a rejected proposal in Metropolis-Hastings) and then the entire block doesn't mix at all in that MCMC iteration.  Increasing tries doesn't fully alleviate the reasons that high-dimensional block sampling can struggle, but it can help.  It looks like this model presents a challenge in how to sample it well.

To increase tries, you would do
HeirOrd2D.Conf$addSampler(target = 'alSpeciesSTAR', type = "RW_block", control = list(tries = 10)) # e.g. 10

Thanks again for the reproducible code.  That was extremely helpful.  I'll file an issue for us to error-trap the internals of how this happened.  It's a little surprising it hasn't manifested like this before.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: ICAR model with NaN WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicky,

I looked at this a bit more based on the reproducible code/data you provided to me off-list.

The numerical issue here is that for some posterior samples, the value of 'u' for a given observation (in combination with the value of 'tau') is such that the (-1,1) truncation interval is far in the right tail of the normal density, and our calculation of the truncated density gives Inf. This is because the truncated density calculation has:  pnorm(1, mn, sd) - pnorm(-1, mn, sd) in the denominator and when the interval is far in the right tail of dnorm(u[i], tau), both of those pnorm values are (numerically on a computer) equal to exactly 1, so nimble divides by 0. The resulting Inf ends up giving NaN for the WAIC. Interestingly, the same underlying issue with truncated density calculations came up in another nimble-users post in the last couple weeks, so this is more evidence that we need to look into seeing if we can make the truncated density calculation more robust.

Back to your statistical problem. I think the fact that this is happening (i.e. extreme 'u[i]' values) relates to poor mixing in your model and relates to using truncation in your likelihood. I would suggest the following changes that will hopefully improve mixing and allow WAIC to be calculated:

1) remove the truncation. Just having the dnorm as the likelihood will result in extreme values of icedata being unlikely (provided the estimated standard deviation ends up being small enough). I don't think you need to explicitly rule out values outside of (-1,1).
2) remove 'alpha' and just have the default 'zero_mean=0'. This treats the overall intercept as being just the (implicit) mean of the phi values. There's some discussion in the nimble user manual about this.
3) I think it may help to have the initial value for tau to be much larger, as the small value you start it at is implausible given the data.

-chris

On Mon, Nov 1, 2021 at 5:50 PM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Vicky,
>
> This would probably be caused by having a likelihood value that is NaN for at least one posterior sample of the parameters and one or more of the observations.
>
> One possibility is that the zero_mean=1 argument is affecting things. This causes the mean of 'u' to be set to 0 after sampling new values of the individual u[i]. However, it's possible that doing that causes the truncation constraint to no longer be satisfied (though I think you should get -Inf, not NaN in that case). So you might try removing alpha from the model and leaving zero_mean at its default value of 0. On a related note, I'll say that you can't really estimate tau0 from the data, as it is informed only by the value of alpha0, which is a scalar and therefore not really informative about a variance parameter. So, just having the mean of the ICAR be estimated implicitly by the mean of the 'u' values is probably a better strategy.
>
> If that's not the issue, one thing you could do is set up the individual steps of creating the model using nimbleModel() and running the MCMC via runMCMC(), making sure to monitor the 'u' and 'tau' variables. You could then take individual posterior samples of those variables and assign them into the model like this:
>
> nodes <- model$getDependencies(c('u','tau'))  # this will include the icedata nodes and any other child nodes of 'u' and 'tau', which should just be the hidden node representing the standard deviation
> model$tau <- out[iteration, 'tau']
> model$u <- out[iteration, <columns with u values>]
> model$calculate(nodes)
>
> to see if you can find the iterations for which the log-likelihood is NaN.
>
> If you're able to share the data so that we can reproduce the error (either on the list or off-list), I can also take a closer look.
>
> -Chris

messages.body_plain:
Daniel, thanks for sending this, it's a helpful summary function indeed.

I just wanted to point out the similarities to the nimble package's own samples summary function:

samplesSummary(samples)
##            Mean     Median    St.Dev.  95%CI_low 95%CI_upp
## mu.n 0.09498151 0.09497028 0.01825259 0.05967935 0.1316005
## sd   0.12761111 0.12641033 0.01317482 0.10505308 0.1570089

which also has a "round" argument:

samplesSummary(samples, round = 3)
##       Mean Median St.Dev. 95%CI_low 95%CI_upp
## mu.n 0.095  0.095   0.018     0.060     0.132
## sd   0.128  0.126   0.013     0.105     0.157

Nimble's samplesSummary() function is similar to your nimSummary() function, although without the "n.eff" and "Rhat" summary statistics.  (The absence of those from samplesSummary is motivated by not having a package dependence on the coda package).  Also, your function concatenates together multiple chains of samples, whereas nimble's samplesSummary only operates on a single chain.  That said, usage to a list of samples from multiple chains can be done as:

lapply(samplesList, samplesSummary)

Also noting that that samplesSummary() function is what nimble's runMCMC() function uses internally to generate the results for the option "summary = TRUE".

As for posterior density and traceplots, from one or more chains of posterior samples, many nimble users make use of (my) "basicMCMCplots" R package, which provides analogous functions:

samplesPlot(...)
chainsSummary(...)
chainsPlot(...)

That said, there are many MCMC plotting packages out there, each offering different aesthetics and functionality.  The functions quoted above are basic, although with a number of useful options available.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.subject: Improving mark-recapture CAR model
messages.body_plain:
All,
I was hoping to get some assistance on improving the speed and convergence of a multiyear mark-recapture CAR model.

Model
A study was conducted on a stream with 17 contiguous strata, where juvenile salmonids were captured, marked, and released. The stream was resampled at a later time where fish marked and unmarked fish were enumerated. If there was no movement between strata, this could be analyzed using a simple Lincoln/Petersen closed population model. However, there was movement between strata and a better approach is to analyzed the data using a Darroch model, which is a multistate model that allows movement or transition between the strata.

Rather than estimate strata adundance (n*) directly, we assume the abundance is a Poisson distributed based on the product of the density (fish/meter) and the area in meters of each strata. I could analyze this as a hierarchical model where log(lambda[i])~Normal(mu_phi,tau_phi). However, this would not account for spatial dependence between adjacent stream reaches, which can be analyzed using a proper CAR model.

To add a level of complexity, I have two years of data that I would like to analyze simultaneously and eventually model density as a function of covariates. The current model has very high autocorrelation, low effective sample size. and poor convergence. Given the model complexity, I could not initialize all nodes and settled for one that would not crash the model. I would appreciate any advice on different samplers or code modification that would improve convergence and speed but am at a loss on where to start given the different distributions and my inexperience with NIMBLE.  Code and data are attached. Thanks!

Dan

messages.subject: DPMM no clustering induced
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Hope your week is going well. Thanks to your help, my previous Dirichlet process mixture model worked.

However, I encountered a problem in running a similar model where no clustering was induced. That is, all the iterations provided the same number of clusters. My DPMM model is a mixture of product of Gaussians, and I apply a Normal-Gamma prior on the mean and precision for each variable. The attached file is the data file I used for the model.

Thank you very much for your help. I will appreciate it a lot.

## ===== DPMM using Nimble =====##
library(nimble)
# a function used to sample from Normal-Gamma distribution
rnormgamma <- function(n, mu0, lambda0, alpha0, beta0) {
  if (length(n) > 1)
    n <- length(n)
  tau <- rgamma(n, alpha0, beta0)
  mu <- rnorm(n, mu0, sqrt(1/(lambda0*tau)))
  data.frame(mu = mu, tau = tau)
}
# DPMM starts here
dat <- read.csv("/fs500.csv")
data <- list(y = dat)
n <- nrow(data$y)
J <- ncol(data$y)

code <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:n] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = n)
  alpha ~ dgamma(shape = 1, rate = 1)
  for(i in 1:n) {
    for(j in 1:J) {
      y[i, j] ~ dnorm(mu[z[i], j], sd = sqrt(1/tau[z[i], j]))
    }
  }
  for(i in 1:n) {
    for(j in 1:J) {
      # set a Normal-Gamma prior NG(3,5, 2,3)
      tau[i, j] ~ dgamma(2, 3) # tau = 1/variance
      mu[i, j] ~ dnorm(3, sd = sqrt(1/(5*tau[i, j])))
    }
  }
})

constants <- list(n = n, J = J)
set.seed(123)
mutau.int <http://mutau.int> <- rnormgamma(J*n, 0,2, 2,1) # generate initial values for mu and tau
inits <- list(z = 1:n, alpha = 1,      # put all the initial values together
              mu = matrix(mutau.int <http://mutau.int>$mu, nrow = n, ncol = J),
              tau = matrix(mutau.int <http://mutau.int>$tau, nrow = n, ncol = J))
model <- nimbleModel(code, data = data, inits = inits, constants = constants,
                     dimensions = list(mu = c(n, J), tau = c(n, J)))
cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
conf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = c('z', 'alpha', 'mu', 'tau'), print = TRUE)
mcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
cmcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc, project = model)
samples <- runMCMC(cmcmc, niter=10000, nburnin = 2000, thin=10)
zSamples <- samples[, grep('z', colnames(samples))]    # samples of cluster IDs
nGroups <- apply(zSamples, 1, function(x)  length(unique(x)))
concSamples <- samples[, grep('alpha', colnames(samples))]
muSamples <- samples[, grep('mu', colnames(samples))]
tauSamples <- samples[, grep('tau', colnames(samples))]
table(nGroups) # almost all of the iterations would favor 2 (or 1)

Hi Meng,

I hope this email finds you well!
It is great to see that you are using nimble, especially the BNP functionality :)

I ran your code and it seems to be working fine. If you run just a few iterations, you will see that the number of clusters and cluster parameters are being updated. Initially you have n clusters (you assigned each observation to a different cluster) and this number rapidly reduces to 9, 5, 4, and then 2 or 1. Also, the means for the “occupied clusters” are around 11, 58, 178, and 374, which are very different from your starting values. So I think the samplers are working fine.

I would take a closer look at your data set. The first column seems to be uniform on [0, 500] and so maybe the results are not so off?

I hope this helps.
Please, let me know if you have more questions.

Best,
Claudia

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I looked through your code and ran it.  I don't know this model well, but I think I roughly followed it.

I don't see something that is not working in terms of MCMC machinery or obvious changes in strategy.  Your chains looked very short to me.  I ran them for much longer (10x, and you might consider 100x), with some thinning (and possibly use monitors2 as well), and lots of nodes seemed to be mixing.

I did not see mixing for most of the theta elements, but that seemed to make sense.  It looks like those are sets of Dirichlet-distributed vectors with priors making it extremely likely that there is no movement between strata, so there will be one 1 and the rest 0, or nearly so, in each vector.  That makes sense because the data seem to show only a handful of movements between strata.  I am not clear if there is much information in the data on movement and hence much useful estimation that can happen here or if you are comfortable more or less imposing the movement probabilities or if I'm not following this part.  But from an MCMC perspective, it seems to make sense that when there are mostly 0s for how many fish moved strata, and when the prior says strongly that there is nearly no chance of moving, then the posterior will say there is nearly no chance of moving, and all of those theta elements be essentially 0 all the time.  If I look at a cell of theta corresponding (I think) to some of the few movements in the data (e.g. "theta[2, 4, 7]"), it mixes with non-zero probabilities.

It can be important to initialize all unobserved nodes, but sometimes it works fine not to.

HTH

-Perry

for(i in 1:nvec1){
vec1 ~ dgamma(shape1,rate1)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaume,

Here is one idea.

vec1[i] ~ dgamma_toggle(shape1, rate1, removed[i])

dgamma_toggle <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(x = double(), shape = double(), rate = double(), removed = double(), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
   if(removed == 0)
       logProb <- 0
   else
        logProb <- dgamma(x, shape = shape, rate = rate, log = TRUE)

  if(log)
     return(logProb). ## From a model, log will always be TRUE
   else
      return(exp(logProb))

   returnType(double())
})

This replaces dgamma with a custom version of dgamma that treats removed nodes as unimportant (by always giving them 0 log likelihood).  Then you would not need to create vec2 or vec3, and you can change the entries in removed[] to change which elements of vec1 contribute to the likelihood for shape1 and rate1.

If it is preferable to create vec2, you can use the following trick:

dummy[i] ~ dgamma_dummy(vec2[i], shape1, rate1, removed[i])

and write a nimbleFunction for dgamma_dummy.  Here the dummy[i] values need to be provided as data and will be provided as "x" to dgamma_dummy.  However, dgamma_dummy can ignore them and return dgamma(vec2[i], shape1, rate = rate1, log = TRUE) (when removed[i] is FALSE).  This is a way to place a stochastic node (dummy[i]) in the model graph but ignore its value and instead calculate a log probability contribution from other values (vec2[i] in this case).

There is also a way you could do this by turning samplers on and off, but the above seems easier unless the scale of the problem is a computational bottleneck.

Also note that any vec1 nodes with NA values will be assigned samplers in the MCMC configuration step.  If you later give them non-NA values intended as data, after building the MCMC (and/or compiling), those samplers will still be there, so the nodes will be sampled rather than treated like data.  The samplers do not dynamically update what is treated as missing data (NA) or not after that has been determined during MCMC configuration and building.  And vice-versa, if you set a node from non-NA to NA after those steps, it will not dynamically be assigned a sampler.  (What you can do is ensure that all nodes have samplers and then omit the ones you don't want by leaving them out of the sampler order vector. But the above ideas seem easier.)

-Perry

> > > > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> > > >
> > > > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> > > >
> > > > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > > > RW samplers: x and y
> > > > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > > > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> > > >
> > > > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > > > branch sampler: x
> > > > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> > > >
> > > > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> > > >
> > > > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> > > >
> > > > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > > > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > > > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > > > Nothing is data.
> > > > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > > > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> > > >
> > > > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > > > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > > > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> > > >
> > > > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> > > >
> > > > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> > > >
> > > > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> > > >
> > > > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> > > >
> > > > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.

> > > > On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 9:31 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > > > > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> > > > >
> > > > > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> > > > >
> > > > > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > > > > RW samplers: x and y
> > > > > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > > > > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> > > > >
> > > > > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > > > > branch sampler: x
> > > > > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> > > > >
> > > > > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> > > > >
> > > > > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> > > > >
> > > > > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > > > > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > > > > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > > > > Nothing is data.
> > > > > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > > > > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> > > > >
> > > > > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > > > > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > > > > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> > > > >
> > > > > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> > > > >
> > > > > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> > > > >
> > > > > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> > > > >
> > > > > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> > > > >
> > > > > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
> > > > >
> > > > > If you still have other questions, don't hesitate to follow up further.
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > Daniel

> > > > > Thanks Daniel, this helps me understand the implications of the changes. Regarding this "hack" specifically, I want nimble to automatically set up samplers as if the capture history is data and then I replace the update for the latent capture histories. This is more or less how it worked before with the exception that nimble specified a posterior predictive update for the latent capture histories that I then replaced. > > > > > On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 9:31 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > > > > > RW samplers: x and y
> > > > > > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > > > > > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > > > > > branch sampler: x
> > > > > > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > > > > > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > > > > > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > > > > > Nothing is data.
> > > > > > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > > > > > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > > > > > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > > > > > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If you still have other questions, don't hesitate to follow up further.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > > Daniel

> > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > > >   #feature observation process
> > > > > > > > > >   for(l in 1:n.samples){
> > > > > > > > > >     for(m in 1:n.cov){
> > > > > > > > > >       G.obs[l,m,1:n.rep] ~ dnorm2(mu=G.true[ID[l],m],tau=tau.obs[m],n.rep = n.rep,na.ind=G.obs.NA.indicator[l,m,1:n.rep]) #custom distribution to skip missing values
> > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > >   }

> > > > > > > > > > })# end model
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > In this model, y.true is the individual by occasion binary capture data. We don't observe ID directly, but we observe some "feature scores" in G.obs, which correlate with individual ID. So y.true needs to be updated on each iteration. I have a custom sampler to do this and it worked in version 0.10.1.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > In version 0.10.1, Nimble will assign a posterior predictive update for y.true, which is incorrect, and I replaced it with an update that is correct. Since I don't have 0.10.1 installed, the following are the samplers assigned except for y.true:

> > > > > > > > > > thin2 = 1: ID, u

> > > > > > > > > > RW sampler (3380)

> > > > > > > > > >   - p
> > > > > > > > > >   -sigma
> > > > > > > > > >   - tau.obs[]  (3 elements)
> > > > > > > > > >   - s[]  (450 elements)
> > > > > > > > > >   - G.true[]  (675 elements)
> > > > > > > > > >   - u[]  (2250 elements)
> > > > > > > > > > conjugate sampler (6)
> > > > > > > > > >   - G.mu[]  (3 elements)
> > > > > > > > > >   - G.tau[]  (3 elements)
> > > > > > > > > > binary sampler (225)
> > > > > > > > > >   - z[]  (225 elements)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > We see we get random walk updates for psi, p, and sigma. As previously stated, nimble will list a posterior predictive update for y.true, and I replaced it.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > In version 0.11.1, nimble does not list a sampler assigned to y.true, but it updates it anyway. When I try to replace the sampler for y.true with my custom sampler and then printSamplers('y.true'), it lists my custom sampler there. But the results are nonsense. I'm 99% sure Nimble is doing both the posterior predicitve update and my custom update because the constraints I impose in the custom update are not maintained.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > A final observation is that the code works fine if I treat y.true as completely known.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > So in summary, I think nimble is assigning a sampler to y.true, but not listing it wherever printSamplers pulls from, and so it can't be removed. But it is still used. Does this sound correct?

> > > > > On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 7:56 PM Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > Thanks Daniel, this helps me understand the implications of the changes. There are a few aspects of partial ID SCR models that I've found no other way to implement in nimble than to "hack" the system a bit to make them work. Regarding this "hack" specifically, I want nimble to automatically set up samplers as if the capture history is data and then I replace the update for the latent capture histories. This is more or less how it worked before with the exception that nimble specified a posterior predictive update for the latent capture histories that I then replaced. Also, I could see all the samplers.

> > > > > > After the change, it appears that I can just set the upstream posterior predictive branch samplers for parameters back to what they would have been assigned if the capture histories were not latent (or whatever else might be more appropriate) in addition to replacing the update for the latent capture histories and it will work as it did before.That appears to be the case comparing some posteriors across versions of nimble for the same data sets.

The first model I mentioned is more or less this model (https://www.pnas.org/content/117/30/17903.short) for genotypes with Normal partial ID covariates instead of categorical ones. The only other difference is that this specific model is built on the Royle-Young (2008) SCR model instead of the most common SCR model. I've previously implemented the genotype version in nimble using the same "hacks" and the results match those from my R-based sampler so I'm quite confident nimble was doing what I intended. It looks like I should test this again with the newest version of nimble.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks again,

> > > > > > Ben
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 9:31 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > > > > > > RW samplers: x and y
> > > > > > > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > > > > > > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > > > > > > branch sampler: x
> > > > > > > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > > > > > > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > > > > > > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > > > > > > Nothing is data.
> > > > > > > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > > > > > > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > > > > > > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > > > > > > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > If you still have other questions, don't hesitate to follow up further.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > > > Daniel

messages.subject: Vector random indexing?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm trying to run the autologistic model from Ch 9.6.1.2 from Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology, Volume II (JAGS code here <https://github.com/mikemeredith/AHM_code/blob/main/AHM2_ch09/AHM2_09.6.1.R>) in Nimble, but am running into an issue with vector random indexing (used to identify neighboring cells in a grid).

I *think* there should be a simple solution to this by writing a nimbleFunction to do the nested indexing (I'm going off this old post: https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/TUs5RCw193M), but I'm hitting a wall and my attempts thus far have been unsuccessful. Can anyone help with this?

Thanks so much! Code below:

Cheers,

Neil

######## AHM 9.6.1.2

library(AHMbook)
library(spdep)
library(nimble)

dat <- AHMbook::simDynoccSpatial(side = 30, nyears = 10, nsurveys = 3,
                                 mean.psi1 = 0.1, range.phi = c(0.5, 0.5),
                                 range.gamma = c(0.2, 0.2), range.p = c(0.4, 0.4),
                                 beta.Xautolog = c(1, 1), seed.XAC = 1, seed = 24,
                                 show.plots = FALSE)

nsites <- dat$side^2
nsurveys <- dat$nsurveys
nyears <- dat$nyears
y <- array(NA, dim = c(nsites, nsurveys, nyears))
for(i in 1:nyears){
  y[,,i] <- dat$umf@y[,(3*i-2):(3*i)]
}

neigh <- spdep::dnearneigh(dat$grid, d1 = 0, d2 = sqrt(2) + 0.1)
str(winnb <- spdep::nb2WB(neigh))
numN <- winnb$num

neighID <- array(NA, dim = c(nsites, 8))
for(i in 1:nsites){
  neighID[i, 1:numN[i]] <- unlist(neigh[i])
}

data <- list(y = y)

constants <- list(nsites = nsites, nsurveys = nsurveys, nyears = nyears,neighID = neighID, numN = numN)

autologistic1 <- nimble::nimbleCode({

  psi1         ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  alpha.lphi   ~ dnorm(0, sd = 3)
  beta.lphi    ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1.5)
  alpha.lgamma ~ dnorm(0, sd = 3)
  beta.lgamma  ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1.5)
  p            ~ dbeta(1, 1)

  # likelihood
  # ecological submodel
  for(i in 1:nsites){
    z[i, 1] ~ dbern(psi1)
    for(t in 2:nyears){
      z[i, t] ~ dbern(z[i, t-1]*phi[i, t-1] + (1 - z[i, t-1])*gamma[i, t-1])
      # compute autocovariate and specificy its effects on phi and gamma

 ### *** problem here with vector random indexing ***
      autocov[i, t] <- sum(z[neighID[i, 1:numN[i]], t-1]) / numN[i]
      logit(phi[i, t-1]) <- alpha.lphi + beta.lphi*autocov[i, t-1]
      logit(gamma[i, t-1]) <- alpha.lgamma + beta.lgamma*autocov[i, t-1]
    }
  }

  # observation model
  for(i in 1:nsites){
    for(j in 1:nsurveys){
      for(t in 1:nyears){
        y[i, j, t] ~ dbern(z[i, t]*p)
      }
    }
  }
})

zst <- array(1, dim = c(nsites, nyears))

inits <- function(){
  list(z = zst, psi1 = rbeta(1, 1, 1), alpha.lphi = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
    beta.lphi = rnorm(1, 0, 1), alpha.lgamma = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
    beta.lgamma = rnorm(1, 0, 1), p = rbeta(1, 1, 1))
}

m <- nimbleModel(code = autologistic1,
                 constants = constants,
                 data = data,
                 inits = inits())

# Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, #nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  #getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse: only scalar random indices are allowed; vector random #indexing found in z[neighID[i, 1:numN[i]], t - 1]
